content: Dysmenorrhoea is a prevalent gynecological condition that affects up to 50% of premenopausal women. Among these, approximately 10% experience symptoms so severe that they are incapacitated for one to three days during each menstrual cycle. Primary dysmenorrhoea refers to menstrual pain that occurs in the absence of any identifiable pelvic pathology. Beta2-adrenoceptor agonists have been explored as a treatment option for primary dysmenorrhoea, but their efficacy and safety remain uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of beta2-adrenoceptor agonists in managing primary dysmenorrhoea. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and EBM Reviews. The last search was performed on August 22, 2011. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared beta2-adrenoceptor agonists with placebo, no treatment, other beta2-adrenoceptor agonists, or conventional treatments in women of reproductive age diagnosed with primary dysmenorrhoea. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted relevant data. Five trials involving a total of 187 women aged 15 to 40 years were included in the analysis. Two trials compared oral isoxsuprine with placebo, while the other three trials evaluated terbutaline oral spray, ritodrine chloride, and oral hydroxyphenyl-orciprenalin against placebo. The studies exhibited significant clinical heterogeneity in terms of the interventions used, the timing of assessments, and the tools employed to measure outcomes. This variability precluded the pooling of data to generate a summary estimate of the effects. One study, which had an unclear risk of bias, reported pain relief with a combination of isoxsuprine, acetaminophen, and caffeine. However, none of the other studies demonstrated any significant clinical difference in effectiveness between beta2-adrenoceptor agonists and placebo. Adverse effects were reported in up to 25% of participants across all studies. These side effects included nausea, vomiting, dizziness, tremors, quivering, and palpitations. The authors concluded that the evidence available from these studies is insufficient to make confident recommendations regarding the use of beta2-adrenoceptor agonists for the treatment of primary dysmenorrhoea. The studies were small in size and carried an unclear to high risk of bias, which limits the reliability of the findings. While one study suggested potential benefits, these must be weighed against the significant and often unacceptable side effects associated with this class of medications. The review highlights the lack of precision and the limitations in the available data.
